source: សៀវភៅស្ដីពីដំណាំដំឡូងមី (Book on Cassava), Part 2, UNDP-supported capacity-building programme for cassava, March 2015
text:
Cambodia grows two broad types of cassava: sweet varieties (lower cyanide/HCN content, suitable for direct food use) and bitter varieties (higher HCN content, requiring processing before consumption; used mainly for starch, industrial use, and animal feed). The source notes that proper cooking (adequate boiling/processing) removes most HCN, making sweet varieties safe to eat, and cites research (Tin and colleagues, 2014) that a variety referred to as 'Kartoil' (also associated with the name KM94) was used by roughly 80% of farmers surveyed in the Pailin border area.

Cassava is described as a tropical crop, generally grown between about 30 degrees North and South latitude, tolerant of low rainfall (suitable from roughly 500mm/year and above) and warm temperatures (around 20°C or higher), while also tolerating high-rainfall conditions (up to roughly 2000mm/year) provided drainage is adequate. Early growth focuses on vine/canopy development before the plant shifts energy into root/tuber bulking.

Named varieties described in this source (largely consistent with varieties already documented from cassava Source G): Kasetsart 50 (KU50) - released in Thailand in 1992 and also known as KM94 in Vietnam, widely grown regionally, with starch content cited around 25.4% and dry matter around 37.5%, green shoots with a purplish tinge and white tuber flesh; Rayong 1; Rayong 72 - released around 2000, starch content cited in the range of 20-25%; and Huay Bong 60. The source also references imported Vietnamese varieties SC5 and SC8 as being used by some farmers, said to be more disease-tolerant, though with somewhat lower yield and starch content than some Thai varieties.

The source also discusses the importance of producing 'clean' (disease-free) planting material through managed seed/stem multiplication gardens, selecting healthy stem cuttings free of pest and disease symptoms, to help sustain productivity as improved varieties are introduced.
caveat: This section substantially overlaps with variety and stem-selection content already documented in cassava Source G (Batch 46), which covers Rayong 1/60/72, KU50, and Huay Bong 60 with a yield/starch comparison table. This file captures only the incremental details specific to this source (SC5/SC8 Vietnamese varieties, the 'Kartoil'/KM94 Pailin-border adoption figure) alongside a condensed restatement of already-known variety facts; it should be cross-referenced against Source G rather than treated as a wholly independent variety catalog.
